newsitem.title: INDIA: Lower India deposit rates may reduce lending rates.
newsitem.headline: Lower India deposit rates may reduce lending rates.

text.p: Measures to ease liquidity widely expected to be announced by the Reserve Bank of India in its upcoming monetary policy statement may not lower lending rates unless deposit rates are also reduced, analysts said on Tuesday.

The RBI is expected to announce cuts in banks' cash reserve requirements on Saturday as part of a series of measures to improve liquidity with the banking system and to signal a cut in interest rates.

Analysts said a reduction in cash reserves, while improving liquidity and providing a signal for lending rates to come down, might not be enough by itself to result in a significant cut in interest rates.
It would have to be accompanied by a cut in deposit rates, they said.
"A reduction in the cap on deposit rates would be a very strong signal to the banking industry on the movement of interest rates," said Anindya Chatterjee, economist at James Capel B&K.

Bank deposit rates in India are partially regulated by the RBI. At present, banks are allowed to offer a maximum of 11 percent per annum for deposits with a maturity up to one year and are free to fix their own rates for longer maturities.
Analysts said the 11 percent cap would have to be brought down if banks were to seriously consider a major cut in their lending rates.
Without a fall in deposit rates, any cut in lending rates would only squeeze bank spreads, analysts said.

"While it is true that the RBI has fixed only a cap and banks can offer lower rates, it is unlikely that they will do so on their own," said Aashish Pitale, manager of debt research at ICICI Securities and Finance Company.
"If the RBI really wants interest rates to come down, I feel it should lower the 11 percent cap," he said.

The RBI has cut banks' cash reserve requirements by two percentage points since April, releasing 79 billion rupees ($2.2 billion) to banks. Two cuts of 50 basis points each were effected in April and May and a one percentage point cut in July. The CRR is currently at 12 percent.
State-run banks, which account for about 80 percent of banking business in India, responded by cutting their lending rates in two rounds.

Profit-making state-run banks shaved their prime lending rates by 50 basis points to 16.0 percent per annum in July after the latest reduction in cash reserves was made and some of them made a further cut of 50 basis points in September.
Prime lending rates charged by private and foreign banks range between 17.5 and 19.0 percent.
Statements by RBI and finance ministry officials that the current interest rates are too high, given an inflation rate of 8.3 percent, have not resulted in any further reductions in prime rates.
